mainTopic: Advice for times of danger (plague and famine), רבי יצחק נפחא's fire teaching of אשו משום חציו, and דוד's halachic question about the stacks of barley
overview: This amud opens with practical advice drawn from the פסוק about the night of מכת בכורות: travel in daylight, and during a plague (דבר) stay indoors. The גמרא explains why a ברייתא brings three פסוקים for this, and it tells us that רבא even shut his windows. In a famine the advice flips: leave the city, even if leaving is risky. More ברייתות follow about the מלאך המות: where to walk on the road, not entering an empty בית הכנסת alone, and what crying or playing dogs signal. Next, רבי יצחק נפחא is pulled between one student who wants הלכה and one who wants אגדה. He gives a single פסוק about fire that satisfies both: הקדוש ברוך הוא will 'pay' for the fire of ציון, and the rule of אשו משום חציו. Finally, the גמרא brings three explanations of what דוד was really asking when he longed for water from בית לחם. It then tests those explanations against the פסוקים, and the challenge to רב נחמן's view continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Enter and leave a place while it is light
steps.stepSummary: A teaching: a person should always arrive at a place and leave it in daylight, based on the פסוק forbidding going out until morning.
steps.simpleTranslation: A person should always enter a place while it is good (daylight) and leave while it is good (daylight), as it says: 'And none of you shall go out of the opening of his house until morning.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states a piece of practical advice: travel in daylight, both when arriving somewhere and when leaving.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase כי טוב recalls the creation of light, where the תורה says the light was good. The proof that one should leave only in daylight comes from the פסוק telling בני ישראל not to leave their houses until morning.

keyTerms.meaning: Always, as a general rule of good conduct
'That it is good', a code word for daylight
As it is stated (introduces a פסוק)

steps.whyThisMatters: This same פסוק becomes the first source in the next ברייתא about staying home during a plague.

phrases.english: A person should always enter at "it is good"
phrases.notes: "It is good" means daylight, since the תורה calls the light good when it was created.

phrases.english: and leave at "it is good",
as it is stated: "And none of you shall go out
phrases.notes: שמות 12:22

phrases.english: of the opening of his house until morning."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion of the פסוק ואתם לא תצאו by drawing a practical lesson from it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One should arrive at and leave a place only in daylight, learned from 'none of you shall go out until morning.'

steps.title: During a plague, stay indoors: three verses
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that when there is a plague in the city one should stay home, and brings three פסוקים as support.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If there is a plague in the city, keep your feet in (stay home), as it says: 'And none of you shall go out of the opening of his house until morning.' And it says: 'Go, my people, enter your rooms and shut your door behind you.' And it says: 'Outside the sword will bereave, and inside the rooms there is terror.'
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא gives a rule: during a plague, limit going out, and it lists three different פסוקים for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק is the same one from Step 1. The ברייתא then adds two more פסוקים with the word ואומר ('and it says'), which will make the גמרא ask why more than one source is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Gather in your feet, meaning stay home
'And it says': brings an additional פסוק

phrases.aramaic: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: דֶּבֶר בָּעִיר – כַּנֵּס רַגְלֶיךָ,
phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: If there is plague in the city, gather your feet,
phrases.notes: He means: stay inside and limit your time outdoors.

phrases.english: as it is stated: "And none of you shall go out
of the opening of his house until morning."
And it says: "Go, my people, enter your rooms,
and shut your door behind you."
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 26:20

phrases.english: And it says: "Outside the sword will bereave,
and in the rooms, terror."
phrases.notes: דברים 32:25

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: דֶּבֶר בָּעִיר – כַּנֵּס רַגְלֶיךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same פסוק from Step 1 for a new rule about plagues, and adds two more פסוקים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: During a plague in the city, one should stay indoors.

steps.title: Why bring extra verses?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא needs the second and third פסוקים.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the point of 'and it says'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא added more פסוקים when the first one already seems to teach the rule. This question sets up the next two steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק already says not to leave the house, so the extra sources look unnecessary. The גמרא assumes each added פסוק must teach something new.

phrases.english: What is the point of "and it says"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the structure of the ברייתא in Step 2.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does each additional פסוק teach that the first one does not?

steps.title: The second verse: the rule applies by day too
steps.stepSummary: The second פסוק teaches that one should stay inside during a plague even in the daytime.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say that this applies only at night, but not during the day, come and hear: 'Go, my people, enter your rooms and shut your door.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the second פסוק: without it, we might think the rule is only at night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק says 'until morning', which could suggest the danger is only at night. The פסוק from ישעיהו says to go inside and close the door with no time limit, so the rule holds by day as well.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say (introduces a possible mistake)

phrases.english: And if you would say: this applies only at night,
phrases.notes: Because the first פסוק says "until morning."

phrases.english: but in the day not;
come and hear: "Go, my people, enter your rooms,
and shut your door."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 3 for the second פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The second פסוק shows the rule applies in the daytime too, not only at night.

steps.title: The third verse: stay inside even if it is frightening there
steps.stepSummary: The third פסוק teaches that even when there is fear inside the house, going outside is more dangerous.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say that this applies only where there is no fear inside, but where there is fear inside it is better to go out and sit among people in company, come and hear: 'Outside the sword will bereave, and in the rooms terror.' Even though there is terror in the rooms, outside the sword will bereave.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the third פסוק: without it, we might think that if the house is frightening, it is better to go be with other people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might think the rule to stay home holds only when home feels safe. The פסוק in דברים mentions both terror inside and the sword outside, showing that even with fear indoors, outside is where death strikes, so one should still stay in.
steps.whatToRemember: During a plague one stays indoors: the first פסוק gives the rule, the second shows it applies by day too, and the third shows it applies even if staying inside is frightening.

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי תֵּימָא: הָנֵי מִילֵּי [הֵיכָא] דְּלֵיכָּא אֵימָה מִגַּוַּאי,
phrases.english: And if you would say: this applies only where there is no fear inside,
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is added in the corrected wording.

phrases.english: but where there is fear inside,
when he goes out and sits among people
in general company, it is better;
come and hear: "Outside the sword will bereave
and in the rooms, terror":
even though in the rooms there is terror,
outside the sword will bereave.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא: הָנֵי מִילֵּי הֵיכָא דְּלֵיכָּא אֵימָה מִגַּוַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues answering Step 3, now explaining the third פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The third פסוק shows that even when there is fear inside, going outside is more dangerous, so one should stay in.

steps.title: רבא closed his windows during a plague
steps.stepSummary: רבא would shut his windows during a plague, based on a פסוק in ירמיהו that describes death coming in through the windows.
steps.simpleTranslation: During a time of plague, רבא used to close the windows of his house, because it says: 'For death has come up into our windows.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports what רבא actually did during a plague. This continues the earlier teaching that one should stay safely inside during a plague.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier steps taught that one should stay indoors. רבא took it a step further: even inside the house, he blocked the windows, because the פסוק describes death entering through them. This is a real-life practice built on reading the פסוק literally.

keyTerms.meaning: A time of anger, meaning a time of plague

phrases.english: Rava, at a time of anger,
phrases.notes: 'Anger' here means a plague, a time when Heaven's anger is out in the world.

phrases.english: would close the windows,
as it is written: 'For death has come up into our windows.'
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 9:20

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא, בְּעִידָּן רִתְחָא הֲוָה סָכַר כַּוֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds an אמורא's practice that extends the ברייתא's rule of staying indoors during a plague.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: During a plague, close the windows, since death can enter through them.

steps.title: In a famine, leave the city
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that during a famine one should leave the city. It brings support from אברהם going down to מצרים and from a פסוק in מלכים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If there is famine in the city, get moving and leave. As it says: 'There was a famine in the land, and אברם went down to מצרים to live there.' And it also says: 'If we say we will go into the city, the famine is in the city and we will die there.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new ברייתא gives the opposite advice from the plague case: in a famine, leave the city instead of staying put. It brings two פסוקים as sources.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a plague, staying home protects you. In a famine, staying means starving, so the safe choice is to leave. The first פסוק shows אברהם leaving during a famine. The second פסוק, introduced with 'and it says', sets up the גמרא's next question.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'spread your feet': leave the place
'And it says': introduces an additional פסוק

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: If there is famine in the city –
spread your feet,
phrases.notes: In other words, get up and leave the city.

phrases.english: as it says: 'And there was a famine in the land,
and Abram went down to Egypt to live there.'
phrases.notes: בראשית 12:10. The word in square brackets is the corrected wording; some versions have the word in round brackets instead.

phrases.english: And it says: 'If we say: We will enter the city,'
phrases.notes: מלכים ב 7:4

phrases.english: then the famine is in the city, and we will die there.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from plague (stay inside) to famine (leave the city).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: During a famine, one should leave the city.

steps.title: Why bring the second verse?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא needed the second פסוק, since the first one already taught to leave in a famine.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the point of 'and it says'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question: what does the second פסוק add? This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story of אברהם already showed that one should leave during a famine. So the second פסוק must be teaching something new, and the גמרא wants to know what.

phrases.english: What is the reason for 'and it says'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the need for the ברייתא's second פסוק, the same way step 3 did for the plague ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What new lesson does the second פסוק teach beyond the first?

steps.title: Leave even when leaving is risky
steps.stepSummary: The second פסוק teaches that one should leave a famine even when the alternative itself carries a risk of death.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have thought the rule to leave applies only when leaving is safe, but not when leaving might put your life at risk. Come and hear: 'Come, let us go over to the camp of ארם; if they let us live, we will live.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question. The second פסוק shows that you should leave the famine even when where you are going is also dangerous.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אברהם going to מצרים might seem like a safe move. But in the second פסוק, the starving men chose to walk into an enemy camp where they might be killed. They did this because staying meant certain death, while going gave them a chance to live.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say: introduces a possible mistaken thought
These words apply: this rule applies only
Come and hear: introduces a source

steps.whatToRemember: In a famine, leave. This holds even if leaving is risky, because staying means certain death while leaving offers a chance to survive.

phrases.english: And if you would say: this applies only
where there is no possible danger to life,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הֵיכָא דְּאִיכָּא סְפֵק נְפָשׁוֹת – לָא;
phrases.english: but where there is a possible danger to life – no;

phrases.aramaic: תָּא שְׁמַע: ״לְכוּ וְנִפְּלָה אֶל מַחֲנֵה אֲרָם,
phrases.english: come and hear: 'Come, and let us go over to the camp of Aram,
if they let us live, we will live.'
phrases.notes: This is the next part of the same פסוק in מלכים ב 7:4. The men knew the enemy might kill them.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא: הָנֵי מִילֵּי הֵיכָא דְּלֵיכָּא סְפֵק נְפָשׁוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 8's question by giving the second פסוק its own lesson.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The second פסוק teaches that one should leave a famine even when leaving involves a possible danger to life.

steps.title: In a plague, avoid the middle of the road
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that during a plague one should not walk in the middle of the road, because the מלאך המות walks there. The גמרא explains this is because he has permission and walks openly.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If there is a plague in the city, a person should not walk in the middle of the road, because the מלאך המות walks in the middle of the roads. Since he has been given permission, he walks openly.
steps.whatsHappening: A new ברייתא gives advice on where to walk during a plague: stay out of the middle of the road. The Aramaic explanation tells us why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: During a plague, the מלאך המות has been given permission to strike, so he has no need to hide and walks openly in the middle. Staying to the side keeps you out of his path.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: If there is a plague in the city –
a person should not walk in the middle of the road,
because the Angel of Death
walks in the middle of the roads.
For since he has been given permission,
phrases.notes: He means permission from Heaven to kill in that city.

phrases.english: he walks openly.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: דֶּבֶר בָּעִיר – אַל יְהַלֵּךְ אָדָם בְּאֶמְצַע הַדֶּרֶךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the plague theme with a new ברייתא about where to walk.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: During a plague, do not walk in the middle of the road.

steps.title: In peaceful times, avoid the sides of the road
steps.stepSummary: The same ברייתא continues: when the city is at peace, avoid the sides of the road. The גמרא explains that without permission, the מלאך המות hides and walks along the sides.
steps.simpleTranslation: If there is peace in the city, do not walk on the sides of the roads. Since he has no permission, he hides himself and walks there.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives the opposite advice for peaceful times: stay away from the sides of the road. The Aramaic explanation says why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without permission, the מלאך המות cannot act openly, so he sneaks along the edges, catching people where he can. So the danger zone flips: in a plague it is the middle, and in peace it is the sides.

keyTerms.meaning: Peace in the city: no plague

steps.whatToRemember: Plague: avoid the middle of the road, where the מלאך המות walks openly. Peace: avoid the sides, where he walks in hiding.

phrases.english: If there is peace in the city –
one should not walk on the sides of the roads.
For since he does not have permission,
he hides himself and walks.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁלוֹם בָּעִיר – אַל יְהַלֵּךְ בְּצִדֵּי דְרָכִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The second half of the same ברייתא, giving the opposite case of step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In peaceful times, do not walk on the sides of the road.

steps.title: During a plague, do not enter a synagogue alone
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that during a plague a person should not go into a בית הכנסת by himself, because the מלאך המות keeps his tools there.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: when there is a plague in the city, a person should not go into the בית הכנסת alone, because the מלאך המות leaves his tools there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא about safety during a plague. This one is about going into a בית הכנסת alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This continues the list from the earlier steps about plague dangers. Steps 10-11 were about where to walk on the road; this one is about a specific place to avoid when you are alone. The reason given is that the מלאך המות stores his tools there.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
If there is a plague in the city,

phrases.aramaic: אַל יִכָּנֵס אָדָם יָחִיד לְבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת,
phrases.english: a person should not go into the synagogue alone,
because the Angel of Death leaves his tools there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another plague-time danger to the list started in steps 10-11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: During a plague, one should not enter a בית הכנסת alone, because the מלאך המות stores his tools there.

steps.title: The synagogue danger applies only when it is empty of learning and prayer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא limits the warning: it applies only when children are not learning there and a מנין is not praying there.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this applies only where young children do not learn in it, and ten men do not pray in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the rule from the last step. The danger is only in an empty בית הכנסת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 12 could sound like every בית הכנסת is dangerous during a plague. This step shows that is not so. If children are learning there or ten men are praying there, it is not a dangerous place.

keyTerms.meaning: And these words apply only... (introduces a limitation)
Ten men, a מנין for prayer

steps.confusionAlert: Do not walk away thinking a בית הכנסת is a dangerous place. The warning is only about being alone in one that is empty of learning and prayer.

phrases.english: And this applies only
where young children do not learn in it,
and ten men do not pray in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָנֵי מִילֵּי הֵיכָא דְּלָא קָרוּ בֵּיהּ דַּרְדְּקֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the rule of step 12 to an empty בית הכנסת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The danger of the בית הכנסת applies only when no children are learning there and no מנין is praying there.

steps.title: What crying dogs and playing dogs signal
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that crying dogs signal the מלאך המות has come to the city, and playing dogs signal אליהו הנביא has come.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: when dogs cry, the מלאך המות has come to the city. When dogs play, אליהו הנביא has come to the city.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא connected to the מלאך המות. This one is about signs we can see in how dogs behave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The topic of the מלאך המות coming to a city leads to this ברייתא. It gives two opposite signs: crying means danger is coming, and playing means a good visitor, אליהו הנביא, has come.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
When dogs are crying,
the Angel of Death has come to the city.
When dogs are playing,
Elijah the prophet has come to the city.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from where the מלאך המות stays to how one can tell he has come.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Crying dogs signal the מלאך המות has come; playing dogs signal אליהו הנביא has come.

steps.title: The dog signs count only when no female dog is around
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא limits the dog signs: they mean something only if there is no female dog among them.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this applies only when there is no female among them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the rule from the last step about dogs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a female dog is there, the crying or playing may simply be because of her. So the signs only count when there is no other ordinary reason for the dogs to act that way.

phrases.english: And this applies only when there is no female among them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the signs of step 14, just as step 13 limited step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The dog signs apply only when there is no female dog among them.

steps.title: Two students pull רבי יצחק נפחא in opposite directions
steps.stepSummary: רב אמי and רב אסי sit before רבי יצחק נפחא. One wants הלכה, the other wants אגדה, and each stops him when he starts teaching the other's choice.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אמי and רב אסי sat before רבי יצחק נפחא. One said to him: Let the Master say הלכה. The other said to him: Let the Master say אגדה. He began to say אגדה, and one did not let him. He began to say הלכה, and the other did not let him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story. Two students each want a different kind of learning, and their teacher gets stuck in the middle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a shift from the plague ברייתות to a story about רבי יצחק נפחא. Each student blocks the other's request, so the teacher cannot teach anything at all. This sets up the משל he gives in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Before him, in front of him
An אגדה teaching, stories and non-legal lessons

phrases.english: Rav Ami and Rav Asi sat
before Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha.

phrases.aramaic: מָר אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לֵימָא מָר שְׁמַעְתְּתָא,
phrases.english: One said to him: Let the Master say halacha,

phrases.aramaic: וּמָר אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לֵימָא מָר אַגָּדְתָּא.
phrases.english: and the other said to him: Let the Master say aggada.
He began to say aggada,
and one of them did not let him.
He began to say halacha,
and the other did not let him.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָתֵיב רַב אַמֵּי וְרַב אַסִּי קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי יִצְחָק נַפָּחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the plague ברייתות and opens a new story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The two students' opposite demands left רבי יצחק נפחא unable to teach either הלכה or אגדה.

steps.title: The parable of the man with two wives
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק נפחא compares his situation to a man with a young wife who pulls out his white hairs and an old wife who pulls out his black hairs, until he is completely bald.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: I will tell you a parable. What is this like? A man who has two wives, one young and one old. The young one pulls out his white hairs, and the old one pulls out his black hairs. In the end he is bald from both sides.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק נפחא answers his two students with a משל. He is setting up a lesson, and the story continues after this with how he moves forward.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each wife wants him to look like her, so each removes the hair she doesn't like. Together they leave him with nothing. In the same way, each student blocking the other means the teacher can teach neither.

phrases.english: He said to them: I will tell you a parable.
What is this like?
A man who has two wives,
one young and one old.
The young one pulls out his white hairs,
the old one pulls out his black hairs.
It turns out he is bald from this side and from that side.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶם: אֶמְשׁוֹל לָכֶם מָשָׁל, לְמָה הַדָּבָר דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The teacher responds to the deadlock described in step 16 with a משל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When two sides each remove what the other wants, the result is that nothing is left.

steps.title: One teaching for both students: God pays for the fire He lit
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק נפחא offers a teaching that fits both students. He reads the פסוק of a fire that 'goes out by itself' as הקדוש ברוך הוא saying He must pay for the fire He lit.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: If so, I will tell you something that fits both of you. 'If a fire goes out and finds thorns' means it goes out by itself. 'The one who lit the fire shall surely pay.' הקדוש ברוך הוא said: It is on Me to pay for the fire that I lit.
steps.whatsHappening: Since each student keeps stopping him, רבי יצחק נפחא picks one פסוק that has both הלכה and אגדה in it. He starts with the אגדה side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says the fire 'goes out' on its own, yet still says the one who lit it must pay. He reads this as a picture of הקדוש ברוך הוא: the fire of the חורבן came because of the people's sins, but God still says He will 'pay' for it.

keyTerms.meaning: the one who lit the fire

phrases.english: He said to them: If so,
I will say to you a matter
that is fitting for both of you:
"If a fire goes out and finds thorns" –
phrases.notes: שמות 22:5

phrases.english: "goes out" means by itself,
"the one who lit the fire shall surely pay."
The Holy One, Blessed be He, said:
It is upon Me to pay for the fire that I lit –

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אֵימָא לְכוּ מִלְּתָא דְּשָׁוְיָא לְתַרְוַיְיכוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the problem described in steps 16-17 by offering a teaching that satisfies both students.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק of fire is read as הקדוש ברוך הוא taking upon Himself to 'pay' for the fire He lit.

steps.title: God burned ציון and will rebuild it with fire
steps.stepSummary: Two פסוקים show what God's 'payment' means: He set fire to ציון, and in the future He will rebuild it with a wall of fire.
steps.simpleTranslation: I set a fire in ציון, as it says: 'And He kindled a fire in ציון and it consumed its foundations.' And I will rebuild it with fire in the future, as it says: 'And I will be for her a wall of fire all around, and I will be the glory in her midst.'
steps.whatsHappening: The אגדה is finished with two פסוקים: one shows God lit the fire, and the other shows how He will 'pay' for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fire in איכה is the destruction. The 'payment' is the future rebuilding, which is also with fire, a protective wall of fire from זכריה. So the damage and the repair match each other.

keyTerms.meaning: will rebuild it in the future

phrases.english: I set a fire in Zion,
as it says: "And He kindled a fire in Zion,
and it consumed its foundations";
phrases.notes: איכה 4:11

phrases.english: and I will in the future build it with fire,
as it says: "And I will be for her
a wall of fire all around,
and I will be the glory in her midst."
phrases.notes: זכריה 2:9

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings פסוקים to show what God lit and how He will 'pay' for it.
steps.raayaObject: God's statement that He will 'pay' for the fire He lit
steps.raayaSupportSource: איכה 4:11 (the fire in ציון) and זכריה 2:9 (the wall of fire)

steps.title: The הלכה: a person's fire is like his arrows
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה half: the פסוק starts with damage by one's property (the fire) and ends with damage by one's body (the one who lit it). This teaches אשו משום חציו.
steps.simpleTranslation: The הלכה: The פסוק began with damage done by his property and ended with damage done by his body, to teach you that his fire is like his arrows.
steps.whatsHappening: Now רבי יצחק נפחא gives the הלכה side of the same פסוק, so the student who wanted הלכה is also satisfied.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'If a fire goes out' sounds like property doing damage on its own, but 'the one who lit the fire shall pay' points to the person himself. So the person is responsible for fire damage as if he did it directly, like shooting an arrow.

keyTerms.meaning: his fire counts like his arrows

steps.whatToRemember: One פסוק gave both students what they wanted: the אגדה of God rebuilding ציון with fire, and the הלכה of אשו משום חציו.
steps.whyThisMatters: אשו משום חציו is a key idea in the laws of fire damage: the one who lit the fire is liable as if he caused the damage himself.

phrases.english: The halacha:
The verse opened with damages caused by his property,
and ended with damages caused by his body;
to tell you: his fire is because of his arrows.
phrases.notes: He means you pay for your fire the same way you pay for an arrow you shot yourself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the הלכה reading of the same פסוק used for the אגדה in step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Liability for fire damage is like liability for arrows: אשו משום חציו.

steps.title: דוד longs for water from the well of בית לחם
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the פסוק where דוד longs for water from the well of בית לחם, and three mighty men break through the פלשתים camp to bring it.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And דוד longed and said: Who will give me water to drink from the well of בית לחם, which is by the gate? And the three mighty men broke through the camp of the פלשתים and drew water from the well of בית לחם, which is by the gate,' and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new אגדה by quoting a פסוק. This is a setup; the explanation of what דוד really wanted comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing is explained yet. The פסוק is quoted so the גמרא can explain right after what דוד was really asking about, since he ended up not drinking the water.

phrases.english: "And David longed and said:
Who will give me water to drink
from the well of Beit Lechem which is by the gate.
And the three mighty men broke through
the camp of the Philistines,
and drew water from the well of Beit Lechem
which is by the gate [etc.]."
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 23:15–16. "וגו׳" means the פסוק keeps going.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַיִּתְאַוֶּה דָוִד וַיֹּאמַר: מִי יַשְׁקֵנִי מַיִם מִבֹּאר בֵּית לֶחֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new אגדה, connected to the fire theme. It is set up here and explained in the next steps.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Quotes the פסוק of דוד's longing as the base text for the coming explanation.

steps.title: What was דוד asking?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what halachic question דוד was raising.
steps.simpleTranslation: What was he asking about?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what question דוד was really asking when he longed for the 'water.' This line sets up the explanations that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא treats דוד's longing in the פסוק as a halachic question, not plain thirst. Now it wants to know the exact topic, and three different answers will follow.

keyTerms.meaning: he was asking / he had a question

phrases.english: What was he asking about?
phrases.notes: 'He' is דוד, from the פסוק about the water of בית לחם in the last step.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what the 'water' in the פסוק of Step 21 stands for.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact halachic topic of דוד's question.

steps.title: First answer: hidden items burned by fire
steps.stepSummary: רבא, quoting רב נחמן, says דוד asked whether the הלכה about טמון באש follows רבי יהודה or the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said in the name of רב נחמן: He was asking about something hidden that got burned in a fire, whether the הלכה follows רבי יהודה or the רבנן. And they answered him whatever they answered him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן says דוד's question was about fire damage to items that were hidden, which is exactly the topic of our sugya.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה holds a person must pay for hidden items burned by his fire, and the רבנן say he does not. דוד wanted to know which view is the הלכה. The גמרא does not tell us the answer, only that they answered him.

keyTerms.meaning: a hidden item damaged by fire
they resolved it for him / they answered him

steps.confusionAlert: Do not look for the answer here. The words 'they answered him what they answered him' mean the גמרא deliberately leaves the answer unstated.

phrases.english: Rava said that Rav Naḥman said:
He was asking about a hidden item in a fire,
whether it follows Rabbi Yehuda or the Rabbis,
phrases.notes: רבי יהודה says you pay for hidden things your fire burned; the רבנן say you don't.

phrases.english: and they answered him what they answered him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first answer to the question of Step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: דוד asked whether the הלכה of טמון באש follows רבי יהודה (liable) or the רבנן (exempt).

steps.title: Second answer: saving yourself with someone else's property
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא says פלשתים were hiding in Jewish barley stacks, and דוד asked whether he could save himself by destroying them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: There were stacks of barley belonging to Jews, and the פלשתים were hiding in them. He asked: May a person save himself by using up someone else's property?
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא gives a different explanation: דוד's question was whether he could burn Jewish barley stacks to defeat the פלשתים hiding inside.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This moves the question from fire damage to a broader rule: may you destroy another person's property to save your own life? The answer comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: to save oneself with another person's property

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
There were stacks of barley belonging to Jews,
and the Philistines were hiding in them,
and he was asking:
May one save himself with another person's property?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, different answer to the question of Step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: דוד asked whether one may destroy another's property to save his own life.

steps.title: Forbidden for others, but a king is different
steps.stepSummary: They answered דוד that saving yourself with another person's property is forbidden, but a king may break through to make a path and no one can stop him.
steps.simpleTranslation: They sent him an answer: It is forbidden to save yourself with someone else's property. But you are a king, and a king may break through to make a path for himself, and no one can stop him.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer to רב הונא's version of the question arrives: normally it is forbidden, but דוד as king is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two rules come out here. A regular person may not save himself by destroying another's property. A king has special power to break through for his path, so for דוד it was permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: breaks through to make himself a path

steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a general rule: a person may not save himself by destroying someone else's property. The king is the exception.

phrases.english: They sent to him:
It is forbidden to save oneself with another person's property;
but you are a king,
and a king may break through to make a path for himself
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is added in the corrected wording; some versions don't have it.

phrases.english: and no one may stop him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in רב הונא's explanation.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Saving oneself with another's property is forbidden, but a king may break through for his path and cannot be stopped.

steps.title: Third answer: trading barley for lentils
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן, or רבה בר מרי, say דוד asked whether he could take a Jew's barley for his animals and pay with the פלשתים's lentils.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן, and some say רבה בר מרי, said: There were stacks of barley belonging to Jews and stacks of lentils belonging to the פלשתים. They asked: May one take the Jews' barley stacks to put in front of his animal, planning to pay back with the פלשתים's lentil stacks?
steps.whatsHappening: A third explanation: דוד wanted to know if he could take a fellow Jew's barley for his animals and repay the owner with lentils taken from the פלשתים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here nobody's life is in danger, and nothing is destroyed without payment. The question is whether you may take a Jew's property without permission if you plan to pay him back with something else.

keyTerms.meaning: some say (another opinion of who said it)
with the plan to pay back

steps.whatToRemember: There are three explanations of דוד's question: טמון באש (רב נחמן), saving oneself with another's property (רב הונא), and taking barley to repay with lentils (the רבנן / רבה בר מרי).

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבָּנַן וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבָּה בַּר מָרִי אָמְרוּ:
phrases.english: And the Rabbis, and some say Rabba bar Mari, said:
There were stacks of barley belonging to Jews,
and stacks of lentils belonging to the Philistines;
and they were asking:
phrases.notes: 'They' here means דוד and his men asking the question.

phrases.aramaic: מַהוּ לִיטּוֹל גְּדִישִׁין שֶׁל שְׂעוֹרִין דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
phrases.english: May one take stacks of barley belonging to Jews
to put before his animal,

phrases.aramaic: עַל מְנָת לְשַׁלֵּם גְּדִישִׁין שֶׁל עֲדָשִׁים דִּפְלִשְׁתִּים?
phrases.english: planning to pay back with stacks of lentils of the Philistines?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּנַן וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבָּה בַּר מָרִי אָמְרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a third answer to the question of Step 22, different from both רב נחמן and רב הונא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: דוד asked whether he could take a Jew's barley for his animals and repay with the פלשתים's lentils.

steps.title: The reply to דוד: one who pays is still wicked, but a king may make a path
steps.stepSummary: The answer sent to דוד, built on a פסוק in יחזקאל: taking someone's property, even with payment, makes a person a רשע, but a king has special permission.
steps.simpleTranslation: They sent him an answer: 'The wicked one returns the pledge and pays back what he stole.' Even though he pays for what he stole, he is still called wicked. But you are a king, and a king may break through to make himself a path, and no one can stop him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the actual reply that was sent to דוד. Here it answers the question as the רבנן explained it in step 26: may he take barley now and pay for it later?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof comes from the פסוק: the person who pays back a robbery is still called a רשע. So paying later does not make taking allowed for a regular person. A king, however, has a special right to break through for his needs.
steps.confusionAlert: Paying for what you take does not make it allowed. The פסוק still calls that person a רשע. Only the king's special right changes the result for דוד.

phrases.english: They sent to him:
"The wicked one returns the pledge,
phrases.notes: יחזקאל 33:15

phrases.english: he pays back what he robbed" –
even though he pays for the stolen item,
he is still wicked.
But you, you are a king,
and a king may break through to make himself a path
and no one can stop him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reply to the question as the רבנן explained it in step 26.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A regular person may not take another's property even with payment; a king may break through to make a path.

steps.title: The two verses about lentils and barley fit the exchange view
steps.stepSummary: The view that דוד wanted to exchange barley for lentils explains why one פסוק says the field was full of lentils and another says barley.
steps.simpleTranslation: It works well for the one who says דוד wanted to exchange: that is why one verse says 'the plot of the field was full of lentils' and another verse says 'the plot of the field was full of barley.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts comparing the explanations against the פסוקים. It shows that the exchange view fits the two verses nicely, and this sets up a question on רב הונא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One verse says lentils and another says barley. If דוד was dealing with both barley (to take) and lentils (to pay with), then both crops really were there. That way the verses don't contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: it works well (for one view); usually followed by 'but' for the other view

phrases.english: Granted, according to the one who says it was to exchange –
phrases.notes: This is the view of the רבנן from step 26: take the barley, pay back with lentils.

phrases.english: that is why one verse writes:
"And there was there a plot of the field
full of lentils,"
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 23:11

phrases.english: and another verse writes:
"And there was a plot of the field
full of barley";
phrases.notes: דברי הימים א 11:13

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts testing the explanations of דוד's question against the פסוקים.
steps.raayaObject: The exchange view of דוד's question
steps.raayaSupportSource: The two verses: one says lentils, one says barley

steps.title: How does the burning view explain the two verses?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רב הונא, who says דוד wanted to burn the barley stacks, explains why the verses mention both lentils and barley.
steps.simpleTranslation: But for the one who says it was to burn, why does he need these two verses?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב הונא. If only barley stacks were involved, why does one verse mention lentils?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exchange view used the lentils as payment. רב הונא's view only talks about burning barley, so the lentils seem to have no role.

phrases.english: But according to the one who says it was to burn,
phrases.notes: This is רב הונא from step 24, who said the stacks hid פלשתים.

phrases.english: why are needed
these two verses?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר לְמִקְלֵי מַאי אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ לְהָנֵי תְּרֵי קְרָאֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the verses that fit the exchange view and challenges the burning view with them.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's view that דוד wanted to burn the stacks
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Burning only involves barley, so the verse about lentils is left unexplained.

steps.title: There were lentil stacks hiding פלשתים too
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא can answer that there were also Jewish lentil stacks where פלשתים were hiding.
steps.simpleTranslation: He can tell you: there were also stacks of lentils belonging to Jews, and the פלשתים were hiding in them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב הונא. Both kinds of stacks were there, and enemies were hiding in both.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lentils don't have to be payment. They can simply be more hiding places, so both verses fit the burning view too.

phrases.english: He can tell you:
there were also stacks of lentils belonging to Jews,
in which the פלשתים were hiding.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge on רב הונא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Expanding the facts: there were two kinds of stacks
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only barley stacks were involved, so the lentils have no place in רב הונא's view.
steps.terutzMaskana: Lentil stacks also hid פלשתים, so both verses fit.

steps.title: 'And he saved it' fits the burning view
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק 'he stood in the middle of the plot and saved it' fits רב הונא's view.
steps.simpleTranslation: It works well for the one who says it was to burn: that is why it says 'He stood in the middle of the plot and saved it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns things around and brings a verse that fits the burning view. This sets up a question on the exchange view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Burning was being considered, and דוד chose not to do it. Then 'he saved it' makes sense: he protected the field instead of burning it.

phrases.english: Granted, according to the one who says it was to burn –
that is why it is written:
"And he stood in the middle of the plot
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 23:12

phrases.english: and saved it";

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר לְמִקְלֵי הַיְינוּ דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a second test, this time using a verse that favors the burning view.
steps.raayaObject: The burning view of דוד's question

steps.title: What does 'and he saved it' mean for the exchange view?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the exchange view explains the word 'and he saved it'.
steps.simpleTranslation: But for the one who says it was to exchange, what does 'and he saved it' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the רבנן's exchange view. If the field was never in danger of burning, what was 'saved'?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the exchange view, דוד was only thinking of taking barley to feed his animals and paying with lentils. Nothing was about to be destroyed, so 'saved it' seems out of place. The answer comes next.

phrases.english: But according to the one who says it was to exchange,
what is "and saved it"?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר לְאַחְלוֹפֵי מַאי וַיַּצִּילֶהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the verse that fits the burning view and challenges the exchange view with it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The רבנן's view that דוד wanted to exchange barley for lentils
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If nothing was going to be destroyed, the word 'saved' has no clear meaning.

steps.title: He saved it by not letting them exchange
steps.stepSummary: The exchange view explains 'and he saved it': דוד stopped the people from swapping the barley for the lentils.
steps.simpleTranslation: He saved it in that he did not let them exchange it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 32. It shows how the exchange view can read the word 'and he saved it'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question was this: if nothing was burned, what did דוד 'save'? The answer is that he saved the field from being swapped: he did not let them exchange the barley for the lentils, so the owners kept their barley.

keyTerms.meaning: and he saved it (the word in the פסוק being explained)

steps.confusionAlert: In this view, 'saved' does not mean rescued from fire or enemies. It means he kept the field from being exchanged.

phrases.english: That he did not let them exchange it.
phrases.notes: This answers 'and he saved it' from the פסוק. The field stayed as it was because no swap was allowed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 32 on behalf of the exchange view.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of a word in the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'And he saved it' seemed to mean a rescue from burning or danger, which fits only רב הונא.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'And he saved it' can mean he kept the field from being exchanged, so it also fits the exchange view.

steps.title: Both views so far explain why there are two verses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא grants that both views covered so far explain why one פסוק says lentils and another says barley. This prepares a challenge to a different view.
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted, according to these two views, that is why two פסוקים are written.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sums up that both views covered so far fit the two different פסוקים. It is setting up its next move. The word 'granted' signals that a challenge to another view is coming.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the exchange view, the two פסוקים name the two crops being swapped, and for רב הונא there were also lentil stacks hiding פלשתים (step 30). The view left out is רב נחמן's (step 23) about טמון באש, and the challenge asking how it explains the two פסוקים comes on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: granted, this works well (usually followed by 'but...')
this is why it is written

steps.confusionAlert: בשלמא is not the end of the discussion. It grants one side so the גמרא can challenge another side right after.

phrases.english: Granted, according to these two views,
phrases.notes: He means the exchange view and רב הונא's view, both covered in the earlier steps.

phrases.english: this is why two verses are written;
phrases.notes: One פסוק says the field was full of lentils, and the other says it was full of barley.

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: קשיא (opening of a challenge against another view)
steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא הָנֵי תַּרְתֵּי, הַיְינוּ דִּכְתִיב תְּרֵי קְרָאֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After both views have been defended, the גמרא sums up that they fit the two פסוקים. This sets up a contrast with another view.
steps.raayaObject: Both views covered so far (the exchange view and רב הונא)
steps.raayaSupportSource: The two separate פסוקים, one naming lentils and one naming barley
